text:
[LSTO.4.6.1] Optional per-write via `ttl: <dur>` on `cache`; expired
keys read as not-found. No TTL means durable until
explicit `cache_delete`. **Nothing evicts it.**

That is worth an author's attention because the opposite
would be easy to assume. A cache under a memory cap does
not make room by discarding an entry: a write that would
breach the cap **fails**, and everything already cached
stays ([RTCT.7.1]). So a key with no TTL is durable in
guarantee and not merely in intent, and a rule may rely on
reading back what it cached.

The cost lands on the writer instead. Under pressure it is
the `cache` action that fails, not a silent loss the reader
discovers later — which is the trade DS wants, since a rule
whose behaviour depended on how full the cache was would
not be reproducible ([LDET.2.1]).
